name: Leaf Spot
symptoms: Brown or black circular spots on leaves
Yellow halos surrounding the spots
Premature yellowing and leaf drop
Spots may merge into larger blotches over time
causes: Fungal pathogens — Cercospora, Alternaria, Septoria
Bacterial pathogens — Xanthomonas, Pseudomonas
Prolonged leaf wetness from overhead watering
Poor air circulation between plants
treatmentOrganic: Remove and destroy affected leaves immediately
Apply neem oil spray every 7 days during outbreaks
Spray copper-based organic fungicide weekly
Improve airflow by thinning dense growth
Apply compost tea as a foliar feed
treatmentChemical: Chlorothalonil fungicide every 7-14 days
Mancozeb for persistent fungal cases
Streptomycin for bacterial leaf spot
Follow label dilution rates — do not over-apply
prevention: Water at soil level, never overhead
Space plants according to mature size for airflow
Rotate crops on a 2-3 year cycle
Mulch to prevent soil-splash onto leaves
Disinfect pruning tools between plants
Avoid handling plants when foliage is wet

name: Powdery Mildew
symptoms: White powdery coating on leaves, stems, and buds
Distorted or curled leaves
Yellowing and premature leaf drop
Reduced flowering and fruit yield
Stunted new growth
causes: Fungal pathogens in the Erysiphales order
High humidity with dry leaf surfaces
Crowded plantings and poor air circulation
Shaded conditions favouring spore germination
treatmentOrganic: Spray 1 tsp baking soda + 1 tsp horticultural oil per 1 L water weekly
Apply diluted milk spray (1 part milk : 9 parts water) every 7 days
Use potassium bicarbonate fungicide weekly
Prune affected leaves and discard (do not compost)
Increase sunlight exposure where possible
treatmentChemical: Sulphur-based fungicide every 10-14 days
Myclobutanil for severe systemic infections
Trifloxystrobin for resistant strains
Rotate fungicide classes to prevent resistance
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars when available
Provide 6+ hours of direct sunlight
Avoid evening watering
Thin foliage for cross-ventilation
Apply preventative neem oil during humid periods

name: Early Blight
symptoms: Concentric dark-brown bullseye lesions on lower leaves first
Yellow halo surrounding each lesion
Defoliation progresses from the base upward
Stem cankers and sunken dark spots on fruit shoulders
Reduced yield and sunscald on exposed fruit
causes: Alternaria solani fungus (and A. tomatophila)
Warm humid weather (24-29 °C) with 6+ hours leaf wetness
Splash-borne conidia from soil and infected debris
Plant stress from poor nutrition, drought, or heavy fruit load
treatmentOrganic: Prune lower infected leaves to slow spread upward
Apply copper-based organic fungicide every 7 days
Spray Bacillus subtilis biofungicide preventatively
Mulch heavily to block soil-splash dispersal
Maintain plant nutrition — healthy plants resist better
treatmentChemical: Chlorothalonil every 7-10 days from first symptoms
Mancozeb on alternating schedule with chlorothalonil
Azoxystrobin as a translaminar option (rotate classes)
prevention: Plant resistant tomato/potato varieties
3+ year rotation away from solanaceous crops
Stake or cage plants to keep foliage off the ground
Water at soil level, never overhead
Destroy crop debris each autumn
Apply preventative sprays during humid weather

name: Late Blight
symptoms: Pale-green water-soaked lesions that expand quickly
White fuzzy sporulation on leaf undersides in humid weather
Brown-black blotches on stems and petioles
Firm brown leathery patches on fruits and tubers
Whole plants can collapse within days of first symptoms
causes: Phytophthora infestans oomycete
Cool wet weather (10-20 °C) with prolonged leaf wetness
Wind-borne spores travel up to 50 km from source
Persists on infected tubers and volunteer plants
treatmentOrganic: Remove and BURN infected plants immediately — never compost
Apply copper hydroxide every 5-7 days at first sign
Spray Bacillus subtilis biofungicide preventatively
Cull volunteer potatoes that emerge after harvest
Stake plants and mulch heavily
treatmentChemical: Cymoxanil + mancozeb for active infections
Metalaxyl-M (systemic) — rotate to prevent resistance
Fluazinam or famoxadone in commercial production
Phosphorous acid drench as a curative
prevention: Choose certified disease-free seed potatoes and transplants
Plant late-blight-resistant varieties (Mountain Magic, Sarpo)
Apply preventative copper sprays before rainy spells
Destroy cull piles and volunteer nightshades each spring
Monitor regional blight reports during cool wet weather
3+ year rotation away from solanaceous crops

name: Rust
symptoms: Orange, yellow, or reddish-brown pustules on leaf undersides
Corresponding yellow flecks on leaf upper surfaces
Premature defoliation in severe infections
Weakened plant vigor and reduced yield
Spore powder rubs off on fingers when touched
causes: Pucciniales fungi — many species, often host-specific
Warm humid conditions (60-75 °F / 15-24 °C) with leaf wetness
Wind-dispersed spores from nearby infected plants
Alternate hosts allowing the rust life cycle to complete
treatmentOrganic: Remove infected leaves at first sign and seal in bin (do not compost)
Spray sulphur dust on cool dry mornings
Apply neem oil every 7-10 days during outbreaks
Use compost tea to boost natural leaf microbiome
Prune for better airflow through the canopy
treatmentChemical: Triadimefon for ornamental rust
Myclobutanil on fruit trees and vegetables
Propiconazole for cereal rusts
Apply at first symptom — curative use is less effective
prevention: Select rust-resistant cultivars
Eliminate nearby alternate hosts (e.g. junipers near apples)
Avoid overhead watering
Space and prune for airflow
Clean up fallen leaves each autumn

name: Wilt
symptoms: Sudden wilting of leaves despite moist soil
Yellowing starting at lower leaves and moving upward
Brown vascular tissue visible when stem is cut
One-sided wilting on tomato/cucurbit plants
Plant death within days to weeks
causes: Fusarium oxysporum (fusarium wilt)
Verticillium dahliae (verticillium wilt)
Erwinia tracheiphila — vectored by cucumber beetles
Soil temperatures above 75 °F / 24 °C favour fusarium
Soil-borne — persists for years in infested soil
treatmentOrganic: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Solarise soil with clear plastic in hot months
Inoculate seedlings with Trichoderma harzianum
Drench root zone with Bacillus subtilis solution
Increase soil organic matter to suppress pathogens
treatmentChemical: No effective curative chemicals — focus on prevention
Pre-plant soil fumigation with metam-sodium (commercial only)
Fungicide drenches with thiophanate-methyl as supportive treatment
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (look for VFN coding on tomatoes)
Rotate non-host crops for 4+ years
Sanitise tools and stakes between seasons
Use clean seed and certified transplants
Avoid over-fertilising with nitrogen
Control insect vectors (cucumber beetles) early

name: Root Rot
symptoms: Wilting despite wet soil
Yellowing lower leaves
Black, mushy, or slimy roots when uprooted
Foul rotting smell from the root ball
Stunted growth and plant decline
causes: Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia, Fusarium fungi
Overwatering and poorly draining soil
Compacted soil restricting oxygen to roots
Reused contaminated pots or potting mix
treatmentOrganic: Stop watering and let soil dry partially
Remove plant, cut away black mushy roots with sterile blade
Repot in fresh well-draining mix with perlite/pumice
Drench with diluted hydrogen peroxide (1 tbsp / L) once
Apply mycorrhizal inoculant to encourage healthy roots
treatmentChemical: Drench with mefenoxam for Pythium/Phytophthora
Etridiazole for ornamental container plants
Thiophanate-methyl for general fungal root rot
prevention: Use pots with drainage holes
Choose well-draining substrate (avoid heavy clay)
Water only when top 2-3 cm of soil is dry
Sterilise reused pots with 10 % bleach solution
Raise garden beds for better drainage
Avoid burying stems below their original soil line

name: Anthracnose
symptoms: Sunken dark lesions on fruit, leaves, and stems
Pink or orange spore masses in lesion centres in humid weather
Premature fruit drop
Twig dieback on woody plants
Leaf curling and distortion on hosts like sycamore and mango
causes: Colletotrichum and Apiognomonia fungi
Warm humid conditions (60-80 °F / 15-27 °C)
Spread via rain splash and contaminated tools
Overwinters in fallen debris and bark cankers
treatmentOrganic: Prune affected branches 15 cm below symptoms
Disinfect tools with 70 % alcohol between cuts
Apply copper-based organic fungicide at bud-break
Mulch heavily to suppress soil-borne spores
Apply Bacillus amyloliquefaciens biofungicide
treatmentChemical: Chlorothalonil at first symptom, every 7-14 days
Azoxystrobin for fruit-bearing crops
Mancozeb for ornamental hosts
Combine with copper for synergy
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars
Rake and destroy fallen leaves and fruit each autumn
Avoid overhead irrigation
Prune for airflow and sunlight penetration
Apply dormant copper spray on woody hosts

name: Black Spot
symptoms: Circular black spots on rose leaves with fringed edges
Yellow halos around spots, leaves turn yellow then drop
Defoliation starts on lower leaves and moves up
Weakened plants with sparse blooms
Cane lesions in severe cases
causes: Diplocarpon rosae fungus
Warm humid weather above 75 °F / 24 °C
Leaf wetness for 7+ continuous hours
Spores splash from infected debris on the soil
treatmentOrganic: Remove every infected leaf — including those on the ground
Spray 1 tbsp baking soda + 1 tsp horticultural oil per 4 L water weekly
Apply sulphur dust on cool dry mornings
Use neem oil every 7-10 days during humid periods
Mulch base with shredded bark to block spore splash
treatmentChemical: Chlorothalonil every 7-10 days
Myclobutanil for systemic protection
Tebuconazole for resistant cases
Rotate three different fungicide classes through the season
prevention: Plant black-spot-resistant rose varieties (Knock Out, Bonica)
Water at soil level in the morning
Provide 6+ hours of full sun
Prune for airflow each spring
Apply preventative dormant-oil + copper spray at bud-break

name: Downy Mildew
symptoms: Pale-yellow angular patches on upper leaf surfaces, bounded by veins
Greyish-white to violet fuzzy sporulation on leaf undersides in humid weather
Lesions turn brown and necrotic as tissue dies
Premature defoliation working from older leaves upward
Stunted growth and reduced fruit or head quality
causes: Oomycete pathogens — Peronospora, Plasmopara, Pseudoperonospora, Bremia species
Cool wet weather (10-22 °C) with prolonged leaf wetness or heavy dew
Wind-dispersed sporangia from infected crops upwind
Overwinters as oospores in soil debris and on volunteer hosts
treatmentOrganic: Remove and destroy infected leaves at first sign — do not compost
Apply copper hydroxide or copper octanoate every 7 days during outbreaks
Spray Bacillus subtilis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens biofungicide preventatively
Drench root zone with phosphorous acid (potassium phosphite) as a plant defence activator
Improve airflow by thinning dense growth and weeding under canopies
treatmentChemical: Mancozeb every 7-10 days as a protectant
Cymoxanil + mancozeb tank mix for active infections
Mefenoxam or metalaxyl-M for systemic control — rotate to prevent resistance
Fluopicolide or mandipropamid in commercial production
Rotate FRAC fungicide groups to delay pathogen resistance
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars where available (DM-resistant cucumber, basil, lettuce)
Water at soil level in the morning so foliage dries quickly
Space plants according to mature size and prune for airflow
Rotate non-host crops on a 2-3 year cycle
Destroy crop debris and volunteer hosts each autumn
Apply preventative copper sprays before forecast cool wet spells

name: Fusarium Wilt
symptoms: Yellowing and wilting starting on one side of the plant or one branch
Lower leaves yellow first, then progressively higher leaves follow
Brown discoloration of vascular tissue visible when stem is cut lengthwise
Wilting during the heat of the day with partial recovery overnight early on
Stunted growth, reduced yield, and eventual plant collapse
Pinkish or white fungal growth on stem base in advanced stages
causes: Fusarium oxysporum soil-borne fungus, with host-specific formae speciales (e.g. f. sp. lycopersici on tomato)
Warm soil temperatures (24-29 °C) that favour fungal growth and infection
Entry through root wounds caused by transplanting, cultivation, or nematodes
Persists in soil as chlamydospores for 10+ years even without a host
treatmentOrganic: Remove and destroy infected plants including the root ball — never compost
Solarise infested soil with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks in hot months
Inoculate seedlings and transplants with Trichoderma harzianum or T. viride
Drench root zone with Bacillus subtilis solution at transplanting
Amend soil with compost to build a suppressive microbial community
Raise soil pH toward 6.5-7.0 with lime (fusarium prefers acidic soils)
treatmentChemical: No effective curative chemicals once a plant is infected
Pre-plant soil fumigation with metam-sodium or chloropicrin (commercial only)
Thiophanate-methyl drench as a supportive treatment on valuable crops
Prothioconazole seed treatment for cereal fusarium species
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars — look for VFN or F coding on tomato seed labels
Rotate to non-host crops for at least 4-5 years
Use certified disease-free seed and transplants from reputable sources
Sanitise tools, stakes, and trellises with 10 % bleach between seasons
Control root-knot nematodes that create entry wounds
Avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser — favour balanced or ammonium-free formulas

name: Mosaic Virus
symptoms: Mottled light- and dark-green or yellow patches on leaves
Leaf distortion — curling, puckering, blistering, or strap-like narrowing
Stunted overall growth and shortened internodes
Reduced flowering and small, malformed, or mottled fruit
Yield loss of 20-90 % depending on virus and infection timing
causes: Plant viruses — Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV), Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV), and many others
Transmitted by sap-feeding insect vectors — aphids, whiteflies, thrips, leafhoppers
Mechanical spread through contaminated tools, hands, and plant-to-plant contact
Seed-borne in some cases (TMV in tomato, BCMV in beans)
treatmentOrganic: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately — there is no cure
Wash hands and disinfect tools with 10 % bleach or 70 % alcohol between plants
Control aphid, whitefly, and thrips vectors with insecticidal soap or neem oil
Release beneficial insects (lacewings, ladybeetles) to suppress vector populations
Use reflective silver mulch to deter incoming aphid vectors
Cover susceptible seedlings with floating row cover until well established
treatmentChemical: No chemical cure exists — viruses cannot be treated with fungicides or bactericides
Manage insect vectors with imidacloprid, pymetrozine, or spirotetramat where labelled
Pyrethroid sprays to knock down adult aphid and whitefly populations
Rotate vector-control insecticide modes of action to delay resistance
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant cultivars (look for TMV, CMV, ToMV resistance codes)
Use certified virus-free seed and transplants
Control weeds — many serve as reservoir hosts for viruses and their vectors
Avoid tobacco products near tomato, pepper, and eggplant plantings (TMV risk)
Disinfect pruning tools between every plant during scouting and harvest
Install fine-mesh insect netting on greenhouse vents and entries

name: Fire Blight
symptoms: Blossoms wilt suddenly and turn brown-black as if scorched by fire
Young shoots wilt and curl into the classic shepherd's-crook shape
Blackened leaves remain attached to dead branches rather than dropping
Sunken, oozing cankers on branches and trunks weeping amber bacterial slime in warm weather
Reddish-brown discoloration of inner bark beneath cankers
Whole-tree death possible on susceptible cultivars within 1-3 seasons
causes: Erwinia amylovora bacterium
Warm humid spring weather (18-29 °C) coinciding with bloom
Spread by rain splash, wind, pollinators, and contaminated pruning tools
Enters through blossoms, natural openings, and fresh wounds from hail or pruning
treatmentOrganic: Prune out infected branches 30 cm below visible symptoms during dry weather
Disinfect pruning tools with 70 % alcohol or 10 % bleach between every cut
Burn or bag and remove all pruned material — never compost
Apply copper hydroxide sprays at silver-tip and green-tip stages
Spray Bacillus subtilis or Aureobasidium pullulans biological products at bloom
Avoid succulent shoot growth — over-fertilising with nitrogen worsens susceptibility
treatmentChemical: Streptomycin sulphate sprays at full bloom where regionally permitted
Oxytetracycline as an alternative to streptomycin in resistant areas
Kasugamycin in commercial orchards under label and regional restrictions
Prohexadione-calcium growth regulator to reduce shoot susceptibility
Rotate antibiotic and biological products to slow resistance development
prevention: Plant resistant pome fruit cultivars (e.g. Liberty, Enterprise, Goldrush apple)
Avoid highly susceptible varieties in regions with frequent fire-blight pressure
Prune in dry winter weather rather than spring or wet conditions
Use minimal nitrogen — vigorous succulent growth is highly susceptible
Monitor regional bloom-time blight risk models (MaryBlyt, Cougarblight)
Eliminate nearby wild hawthorn, mountain ash, and abandoned pome fruits as reservoirs

name: Sooty Mold
symptoms: Black powdery or velvety coating on upper leaf surfaces, stems, and fruit
Coating wipes off with a damp cloth, revealing healthy tissue beneath
Reduced photosynthesis from light-blocking film causing chlorosis and weak growth
Sticky honeydew residue on leaves and on surfaces beneath the plant
Visible aphids, scale, whiteflies, or mealybugs on the plant or nearby
causes: Saprophytic fungi — Capnodium, Cladosporium, Aureobasidium species — growing on honeydew
Honeydew secreted by sap-sucking insects: aphids, scale, whiteflies, mealybugs, psyllids
Warm humid weather that favours fungal colonisation of sugary deposits
Heavy shading and poor airflow that keep honeydew deposits moist longer
treatmentOrganic: Identify and control the honeydew-producing pest first — the mold disappears when the food source stops
Spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil to smother aphids, scale, and whiteflies
Apply neem oil weekly to disrupt pest reproduction and feeding
Release beneficial insects — ladybeetles, lacewings, parasitic wasps
Wash existing mold off leaves with a mild soap-and-water solution and soft cloth
Prune for better airflow and remove ant trails that protect honeydew-producing pests
treatmentChemical: Imidacloprid soil drench for systemic control of sap-feeding pests on ornamentals
Pyriproxyfen or buprofezin for scale and whitefly immature stages
Pyrethroid sprays for quick knockdown of adult aphid and whitefly populations
No fungicide is needed for the mold itself — remove the honeydew source instead
Always rotate insecticide modes of action to delay pest resistance
prevention: Monitor regularly for early signs of aphids, scale, and whiteflies
Maintain healthy plants — well-watered and properly fertilised plants resist pest outbreaks
Control ants that farm and protect aphids and scale from natural enemies
Encourage beneficial insect habitat with companion flowering plants
Prune for airflow and sunlight penetration through the canopy
Hose off honeydew and dust from leaves periodically to discourage colonisation

name: Clubroot
symptoms: Wilting during warm afternoons even when soil is moist
Yellowing, stunted, and poorly developed above-ground growth
Swollen, distorted, club-shaped or spindle-shaped galls on roots
Galls eventually rot, releasing a foul smell and millions of resting spores
Patchy poor stands across brassica beds with healthy plants beside affected ones
Reduced or failed head formation in cabbage, broccoli, and cauliflower
causes: Plasmodiophora brassicae — a soil-borne protist pathogen
Acidic soils (pH below 6.5) and waterlogged conditions strongly favour infection
Soil temperatures of 18-25 °C that promote zoospore movement and root infection
Resting spores survive in soil for 15-20 years and spread on tools, boots, and infected transplants
treatmentOrganic: Remove and destroy infected plants including all root galls — never compost
Raise soil pH to 7.2 or higher with agricultural lime or hydrated lime well before planting
Improve drainage with raised beds and organic matter additions
Apply Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma biological soil treatments at transplant
Bait crop method — fast-growing brassicas tilled in early to stimulate and waste spores
Grow on a long rotation away from all brassica family crops and weeds
treatmentChemical: Fluazinam soil treatment at transplanting in commercial brassica production
Cyazofamid pre-plant drench where regionally registered
No truly curative chemical exists — management focuses on suppression
Always follow regional label restrictions for brassica soil-applied fungicides
prevention: Rotate brassica crops on a 7+ year cycle away from infested ground
Lime soil to pH 7.2-7.4 several months before planting brassicas
Plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (e.g. Kilaton, Crispus, Clapton cabbages)
Start with clean certified transplants — never accept stock from infested nurseries
Clean soil from tools, boots, and machinery between fields and between gardens
Control brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard) that maintain spore populations

name: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN)
symptoms: Chlorotic mottling on young leaves, starting at whorl
Severe leaf necrosis from leaf margin inward
Stunted growth and dead-heart symptom in seedlings
Premature plant death often before tasselling
Cobs malformed or absent — near-total yield loss possible
causes: Synergistic co-infection of Maize Chlorotic Mottle Virus (MCMV) and a potyvirus (SCMV / MDMV / WSMV)
Vector-spread by thrips, leaf beetles, and rootworms
Seed-borne transmission of MCMV
Continuous maize cropping without rotation
treatmentOrganic: Rogue and burn infected plants as soon as symptoms appear
Rotate to non-cereal crops (legumes, cassava) for 2+ seasons
Use certified MCMV-free seed
Encourage thrips predators with diverse field borders
treatmentChemical: No curative chemistry — virus complex cannot be sprayed away
Targeted insecticides for thrips and beetle vectors only as preventive (e.g. lambda-cyhalothrin per label)
Seed treatments to suppress early vector landings
prevention: Plant MLN-tolerant maize varieties where available (KDV1, WE3127, etc.)
Strict crop rotation — do not plant maize on maize
Synchronised regional planting to break vector population build-up
Eliminate volunteer maize between seasons
Inspect seedlings at V3-V5 for the diagnostic dead-heart

name: Cassava Mosaic Disease (CMD)
symptoms: Yellow-green chlorotic mosaic on cassava leaves
Leaf distortion and reduced leaf size
Stunted plant growth
Reduced tuber size and yield (30-90% losses)
Symptom severity worse on young leaves than older ones
causes: African cassava mosaic virus (ACMV) and East African cassava mosaic virus (EACMV)
Transmitted by whitefly Bemisia tabaci
Spread through infected stem cuttings used for planting
treatmentOrganic: Rogue and destroy infected plants — do not replant cuttings from symptomatic plants
Use clean planting material from disease-free fields
Control whitefly vectors with neem oil and yellow sticky traps
Intercrop with non-host plants to disrupt whitefly movement
treatmentChemical: No curative chemistry available for the virus
Whitefly insecticides (imidacloprid, acetamiprid per label) as vector control only
prevention: Plant CMD-resistant varieties (TME 419, TME 14, TMS 30572)
Source cuttings from certified clean-stem schemes
Inspect and remove infected plants at 4-6 weeks after planting
Maintain field hygiene — do not handle healthy plants after symptomatic ones
Rotate fields between cassava cycles

name: Cassava Brown Streak Disease (CBSD)
symptoms: Brown necrotic streaks on stems and petioles
Yellow blotching and feathery chlorosis on mature leaves
Dark brown corky necrosis inside tubers (the diagnostic sign)
Reduced root size and inedible tuber flesh
Yield losses 30-100% in susceptible varieties
causes: Cassava brown streak virus (CBSV) and Ugandan cassava brown streak virus (UCBSV)
Transmitted by whitefly Bemisia tabaci
Spread through infected stem cuttings
treatmentOrganic: Rogue and destroy infected plants and unmarketable roots
Use clean planting material from certified sources
Inspect tubers at harvest — symptoms often only visible internally
Control whitefly with neem and yellow traps
treatmentChemical: No virus-curative treatment available
Whitefly vector control only as preventive
prevention: Plant CBSD-tolerant varieties (NASE 14, MM06/0083, etc.)
Source cuttings from disease-free regions
Early harvest (8-10 months) where pressure is high to reduce tuber necrosis
Maintain regional clean-seed schemes
Avoid moving planting material across CBSD pressure zones

name: Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia)
symptoms: Sudden wilting of one or more branches during the hottest part of the day
Wilted leaves remain green initially, then yellow and collapse
Brown vascular discoloration in stem cross-section
White bacterial ooze when cut stem is submerged in clean water
Plant death within days to weeks
causes: Ralstonia solanacearum — soilborne bacterium
Spreads via contaminated soil, tools, water, and infected plant material
Survives in roots of weeds and solanaceous crops
Favoured by warm (24-35 °C), wet soils
treatmentOrganic: No effective organic cure once symptoms appear
Rogue and destroy infected plants — do not compost
Solarise soil under clear plastic for 4-6 weeks in hot months
Drench infected areas with bleach solution (per safety guidance) before replanting
treatmentChemical: Streptomycin or copper-based bactericides offer limited suppression only
No curative chemistry — focus on quarantine and resistant varieties
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties (especially in tomato, banana, ginger)
Long crop rotation (4+ years) away from solanaceous and host crops
Disinfect tools with bleach between plants
Use clean planting material and certified seed
Avoid water-splash from infected areas — drip irrigation preferred
Manage soil drainage to reduce root injury

name: Black Sigatoka
symptoms: Initially small dark streaks on young leaves, parallel to veins
Streaks enlarge into elongated black lesions with yellow halos
Lesions coalesce, killing entire leaf surface
Severe defoliation leads to premature fruit ripening and bunch loss
Reduces bunch weight by 30-50% in untreated plantations
causes: Fungus Pseudocercospora fijiensis (formerly Mycosphaerella fijiensis)
Spreads by windborne ascospores during wet conditions
Survives on leaf debris between crop cycles
treatmentOrganic: Strip and destroy infected leaves (de-leafing every 2-3 weeks)
Improve plantation airflow with proper plant spacing
Foliar mineral oil sprays where permitted
Avoid overhead irrigation
treatmentChemical: Rotated systemic fungicides — propiconazole, tebuconazole, azoxystrobin
Add protectant mancozeb or chlorothalonil in heavy pressure
Follow fungicide resistance management — never repeat the same class consecutively
prevention: Plant tolerant varieties (FHIA hybrids where adapted)
Maintain healthy plant nutrition (K, Mg)
Manage drainage to reduce humidity
Sanitation — remove infected leaves continuously
Quarantine new planting material from outside the farm

name: Tuta Damage (Tomato Leafminer)
symptoms: Irregular blotch-shaped mines in tomato leaves
Larval frass visible inside leaf mines
Holes bored into stems, flowers, and developing fruit
Fruit damage allows secondary rot organisms in
Severe leaf damage causes premature defoliation
causes: Larval feeding by Tuta absoluta (tomato leafminer moth)
Continuous tomato cropping without break
Mild winters allow year-round populations
treatmentOrganic: Pheromone traps for monitoring and mass-trapping (Tuta absoluta pheromone)
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) sprays targeting young larvae
Spinosad sprays per organic label
Release the parasitoid Trichogramma achaeae where available
Remove and destroy heavily mined leaves and damaged fruit
treatmentChemical: Rotated chemistry — emamectin benzoate, chlorantraniliprole, indoxacarb
Avoid repeated use of pyrethroids (rapid resistance)
Always follow pre-harvest interval (PHI) on the label
prevention: Insect-proof nets on greenhouse vents (mesh ≤0.4 mm)
Crop rotation away from tomato and other solanaceous crops
Destroy crop residues immediately after harvest
Sanitation between seasons — remove volunteer tomatoes and host weeds
Source nursery plants from monitored, treatment-history-known suppliers

name: Cocoa Black Pod
symptoms: Dark brown to black water-soaked spots on cocoa pods
Spots spread rapidly to engulf the entire pod within days
Pods turn hard, black, and shrivelled (mummified)
White fungal growth on lesion surface in humid conditions
Beans inside become rotten and inedible
causes: Phytophthora palmivora and P. megakarya — soilborne oomycetes
Spread by rain splash, ants, and contaminated tools
Favoured by humid, wet conditions and dense canopy
treatmentOrganic: Frequent pod sanitation — remove and bury infected pods weekly
Prune cocoa canopy to improve airflow and light penetration
Copper-based organic fungicides during peak rainy season
treatmentChemical: Metalaxyl + mancozeb foliar spray every 3-4 weeks during peak humidity
Cymoxanil or fosetyl-aluminium where available
Always follow PHI for cocoa export markets
prevention: Plant tolerant clones (CCN-51, ICS-95 where adapted)
Continuous pod sanitation — never leave infected pods on tree or ground
Improve drainage to reduce surface water and splash
Disinfect harvesting tools between trees
Manage shade — too much shade favours the pathogen

name: Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus (CSSVD)
symptoms: Red flushing of young leaves followed by chlorotic mottling
Swelling of stems and roots ('swollen shoots')
Reduced pod size and number
Tree dieback within 2-4 years of infection
Severe yield loss; eventual tree death
causes: Cocoa swollen shoot virus (CSSV) — Badnavirus family
Transmitted by mealybugs (Planococcoides njalensis and related species)
Spread by infected planting material
treatmentOrganic: Cutting-out — rogue infected and contact trees within 15 m radius
Control mealybug vectors with neem oil and natural enemies
Replant cleared sites only after a fallow period of 6+ months
treatmentChemical: No virus-curative treatment exists
Targeted mealybug control with imidacloprid soil drench where labelled
prevention: Plant CSSV-tolerant varieties where available
Source planting material from certified disease-free nurseries
Regular survey of farms — early detection minimises spread
Maintain shade-tree diversity to disrupt mealybug movement
Strict cutting-out programmes coordinated across neighbouring farms

name: Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV)
symptoms: Severe stunting with new leaves becoming progressively shorter and narrower
Bunchy rosette appearance at top of plant ('bunchy top')
Dark green hook-shaped streaks along leaf veins and midribs
Wavy or sawtooth leaf margins
No bunch produced from infected plants
causes: Banana bunchy top virus (BBTV) — Nanovirus family
